fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says, “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua…” (Judges 2:7). Joshua took over leading Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1–2). So picture a whole stretch of days with the people serving the LORD. I'd bake a double batch for a run like that.

Here's what the text says: “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua…” (Judges 2:7). Joshua led Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1–2). So through all his days, the people were serving the LORD. Enjoy this bright spot, because the story is about to turn.

Yes, friend. The text says the people served the LORD through the days of Joshua “…and of the elders who outlived him…” (Judges 2:7). The verse describes those elders as “…who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel.” So the serving ran through the days of Joshua and those elders. Keep that in your back pocket, because it matters in a few verses.

Victory is what you'd hope for when marching out, friend. But the text says the hand of the LORD was against them “…to bring calamity…” (Judges 2:15). Calamity is the word the verse uses. Nobody pulls a fresh batch out of the oven expecting that.

Shiloh isn't in this passage, baker. The text says the LORD “…raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them.” (Judges 2:16). Saving is the job named here. Israel is plundered in verse 14, and by verse 16 the LORD raises up judges. That's a quick turn in the story.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods.” (Judges 3:6). Marriages going both ways, and then serving their gods. I think this one is a sad note to end on.
